section.title: Arise, Shine
section.sectionRationale: This is one of Isaiah's most luminous chapters, Zion's light has come and the glory of the LORD rises upon her, drawing nations, kings, camels laden with gold and frankincense, streaming toward her. It closes with a promise that reaches beyond any earthly restoration, the LORD Himself as everlasting light, a promise John will later borrow to describe the new Jerusalem.
section.thesis: Though darkness covers the earth, the LORD's glory will rise upon Zion and draw the nations and their kings to her light, until He Himself becomes her everlasting light, ending the need for sun or moon altogether.
section.frameNote: Three movements: arise, shine, for your light has come; nations and wealth streaming to Zion's light; and the LORD Himself as everlasting light, sorrow ended forever.

units.label: Arise, shine, for your light has come
units.note: the glory of the LORD rises upon you

verses.text: Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you.
For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness is over the peoples; but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you.
Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.
Lift up your eyes and look around: They all gather and come to you; your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on the arm.

units.label: Gold and frankincense, camels of Midian
units.note: nations and kings stream to Zion

verses.text: Then you will look and be radiant, and your heart will tremble and swell with joy, because the riches of the sea will be brought to you, and the wealth of the nations will come to you.
Caravans of camels will cover your land, young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and {{levonah|frankincense}} and proclaiming the praises of the LORD.
All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance; I will adorn My glorious house.
Who are these who fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters?

Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead, to bring your children from afar, with their silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you.
Foreigners will rebuild your walls, and their kings will serve you. Although I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy.
Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night, so that the wealth of the nations may be brought into you, with their kings being led in procession.
For the nation or kingdom that will not serve you will perish; it will be utterly destroyed.
The glory of Lebanon will come to you, its cypress, elm, and boxwood together, to adorn the place of My sanctuary, and I will glorify the place of My feet.
The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you; all who reviled you will fall facedown at your feet and call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.

units.label: The LORD your everlasting light
units.note: no more sun or moon; sorrow ends

verses.text: Whereas you have been forsaken and despised, with no one passing through, I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age.
You will drink the milk of nations and nurse at the breasts of royalty; you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones. I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler.
No longer will violence be heard in your land, nor ruin or destruction within your borders. But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise.
No longer will the sun be your light by day, nor the brightness of the moon shine on your night; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor.
Your sun will no longer set, and your moon will not wane; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and the days of your sorrow will cease.
Then all your people will be righteous; they will possess the land forever; they are the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified.
The least of you will become a thousand, and the smallest a mighty nation. I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly.

levonah.gloss: Frankincense, a fragrant resin used in temple worship and offered as a costly gift. Paired here with gold in gifts brought by nations to Zion's light, it is echoed almost exactly when Magi from the east bring gold and frankincense, and myrrh, to the infant Christ, Matthew 2:11, treating Him as the true light the nations stream toward.

basic.context: While darkness covers the earth and its peoples, Zion is told to arise and shine because the LORD's own glory has risen upon her. Nations and their kings stream toward that light, bringing gold, frankincense, and their wealth, until finally God Himself promises to become her everlasting light, ending the very need for sun or moon.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, historical hope for Jerusalem's future glory and the ingathering of the nations, drawing on ancient Near Eastern trade routes and treasures familiar to its first hearers. Yet its language, an everlasting light replacing sun and moon, deliberately outgrows any merely historical city and reaches toward the final new creation.
basic.originalLanguages: The nations bring gold and levonah, frankincense, valuable trade goods and worship offerings together, exactly the gifts later brought by Magi to the infant Jesus, Matthew 2:11, treating Him as the very light this chapter describes the nations streaming toward.
basic.typology: The gold and frankincense brought by nations anticipates the Magi's gifts to Christ. The LORD as everlasting light, replacing sun and moon, is quoted almost verbatim by John describing the new Jerusalem, where the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb, Revelation 21:23-25.
basic.christ: Matthew deliberately echoes this chapter when Gentile Magi arrive bearing gold and frankincense to worship the infant Jesus, presenting Him as the light the nations were always meant to stream toward, Matthew 2:1-11. And Revelation 21:23-25 lifts this chapter's language almost word for word to describe the new Jerusalem, where Christ the Lamb is its everlasting light.
basic.god: God is both the one who struck Zion in anger and the one who shows her mercy and glorifies her beyond her former shame; His discipline and His restoration are not opposing impulses but part of one redemptive purpose that ends in Him becoming, personally, His people's everlasting light.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 2:1-11 has Gentile Magi bring gold and frankincense to the infant Jesus. Revelation 21:23-25 describes the new Jerusalem needing no sun or moon because God's glory and the Lamb are its light. Revelation 21:24-26 has the kings of the earth bring their glory into the holy city, echoing verse 11's open gates.
basic.oneStory: A city once forsaken and despised is promised such glory that nations and their kings will stream toward her light bearing their treasure, until the LORD Himself becomes that light forever. That promise, echoed by Magi bringing gold and frankincense to Bethlehem and by John's vision of the new Jerusalem needing no sun, traces one story of God's glory drawing every nation home.

context.literary:
Isaiah 60 is one sustained address to a feminine singular 'you', Zion personified as a woman, and nearly every verb in the first half is an instruction to her: arise, shine, lift up your eyes, look around. The chapter is shaped like a set of widening circles. Verses 1 to 3 give the cause, the LORD's glory has risen and the nations are drawn. Verses 4 to 9 show the movement toward her, first children carried home, then wealth, then caravans from the south and east and ships from the west. Verses 10 to 14 turn to what the foreigners do when they arrive: they build, serve, bring timber and bow. Verses 15 to 18 describe what the LORD does to the city itself, replacing metals with better metals and violence with peace. Verses 19 to 22 return to the opening image of light and carry it to its limit, a city that no longer needs the sun.

The frame is an inclusio. The chapter begins with light, glory and nations coming to the brightness, verses 1 to 3, and ends with the LORD as everlasting light and a people who are the work of His hands so that He may be glorified, verses 19 to 21. In between, the central movement is a series of reversals marked by 'instead of' and 'no longer': forsaken becomes a pride, bronze becomes gold, violence becomes salvation and praise in the names of walls and gates, verses 15 to 18.

The chapter is also tightly linked to the passages around it. 'Lift up your eyes and look around. They all gather together; they come to you' in verse 4 repeats the wording of Isaiah 49:18, which shows chapter 60 delivering the promise made there. The darkness of 59:9 is met by the light of 60:1, and chapter 61 will turn from the city to the person who announces good news. Read in order, the three chapters move from confession, to arrival, to the one who brings it about.
context.historical:
The goods listed in verses 6 to 9 are drawn from the trade routes the first hearers knew. Midian and Ephah are names from the line of Abraham's wife Keturah, Genesis 25:1-4, and Sheba comes from the same family through Jokshan. Kedar and Nebaioth are sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13. The camel caravans carrying gold and frankincense from the south of Arabia recall the visit of the queen of Sheba to Solomon, 1 Kings 10:1-2, and Jeremiah's complaint that frankincense from Sheba is wasted if offered without a faithful heart, Jeremiah 6:20. Ships of Tarshish brought gold and silver in Solomon's day, 1 Kings 10:22. In every case the wealth comes from peoples at the edge of the known world.

It is striking that several of these peoples descend from Abraham's other sons and from Ishmael. The flocks of Kedar and Nebaioth go up on God's altar, so that lines once outside the covenant are brought in as worshippers. The picture is of the family of Abraham reassembled, which fits the older promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed.

The setting is a Jerusalem that had been destroyed and was being rebuilt. Those who returned found a modest temple, and Ezra 3:12 records that many of the older people wept at the foundation while others shouted for joy. Nehemiah found the walls in ruins and the gates burned, Nehemiah 2:17. Against that background, a promise of overflowing wealth and gates that never close would sound extravagant, and the prophet knows it. Persian rulers did pay for the work in the early years, Ezra 6:8-9, which gives a small taste of verse 10, where foreigners rebuild the walls. Yet Haggai had to tell the community that the glory of the latter house would exceed the former, Haggai 2:7-9, because the greater fulfilment had not come. The chapter is addressed to people who could see how much remained undone.
context.canonical:
The prophets repeatedly picture the nations coming to Zion. Isaiah 2:2-3 sees all nations stream to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 49:22-23 has the nations carrying home Zion's sons and daughters, and Isaiah 56:6-8 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will have their offerings accepted on His altar, with the house called a house of prayer for all peoples. Chapter 60 takes all of this and makes it a single, glowing scene. Zechariah 8:20-23 and Haggai 2:7-9 tell the same story, with treasures of the nations filling the house.

Light is the great organizing image. The people walking in darkness who see a great light in Isaiah 9:2 are the first picture, and Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6 make the Servant a light to the nations. Matthew uses Isaiah 9:2 of Jesus' ministry in Galilee, Matthew 4:15-16, and Simeon calls the child 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles', Luke 2:32. Jesus declares 'I am the light of the world', John 8:12, and then tells His followers 'You are the light of the world', Matthew 5:14, so that the light that rises on Zion is also lit in those who belong to Him, Philippians 2:15.

At the end of the Bible, Revelation 21 and 22 reads Isaiah 60 almost line by line. The city has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp, the nations walk by its light, the kings bring their glory into it, its gates are never shut, and there is no more night, Revelation 21:23-26 and 22:5. John has made one change: the LORD who will be the everlasting light of verse 19 is now seen as God and the Lamb together. The chapter therefore forms one thread between the exile, the Gentile mission and the new Jerusalem.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah's first aim was to put heart into a people who had come home to a small and troubled city and could not see how God's great promises could possibly come true. He does not play down the darkness. Verse 2 says plainly that thick darkness covers the peoples. But he insists that the darkness is not the last word, because the LORD Himself is rising on Zion, and that fact will be seen from far away.

He also meant to enlarge their sense of who the people of God are and what they are for. Zion is not a fortress that keeps the nations out. It is a lamp that draws them in, and the nations arrive to worship, to bring praise to the LORD, and to join in building. The gates are open day and night. Israel is meant to understand that its own restoration serves the purpose of God's glory among all peoples, 'so that I may be glorified,' verse 21.

A third aim lies in verses 10 and 15 to 16. The prophet admits that God struck Zion in anger, and then says that in favour He will show mercy. The history of judgment is not hidden, but it is placed inside a longer purpose. Israel is meant to receive the promise without forgetting why the exile happened, and to know that the One who struck is the same One who restores. Finally, verse 22 asks for patience and trust: the matter will happen 'in its time', and yet He will do it 'quickly'. The first hearers were meant to wait without despair.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is almost entirely promise. It describes what God will do and what will happen to Zion, with only one command, the opening 'Arise, shine'. Even that is a command grounded in a fact already declared: 'your light has come.' Nothing here tells readers to build an empire or to expect tribute from foreigners as a right. Verses 12 and 14 speak of nations that refuse to serve and of oppressors bowing, and these are statements of what God will do when He establishes His city, not instructions to the church to dominate its neighbours. The New Testament gives the church the opposite posture of service, Mark 10:45, and of blessing those who persecute, Romans 12:14.

What does carry over to the present is a pattern for how a community of God's people understands itself. It is to shine with a light that is not its own, as Jesus says in Matthew 5:16, so that others see and give glory to the Father. It is to keep its gates open to the stranger. And it is to hold on to a hope bigger than its present circumstances. The chapter also gives a model for prayer in hard times, to pray out of what God has promised and not out of what can currently be seen.

debates.question: When and how is Isaiah 60 fulfilled?

views.label: In the return and rebuilding of Jerusalem
views.case: The first hearers lived after the exile, and the chapter speaks of walls, gates, timber from Lebanon and a glorious house, verses 10 to 13. Persian support for the temple, Ezra 6:8-9, and the later rebuilding of the walls fit these details. On this view the prophet describes the restoration in glowing terms, with some of the language heightened by poetry.

views.label: In Christ and the church
views.case: The New Testament takes up the language of light and nations. Jesus is the light, John 8:12, Gentile Magi come bearing gifts, Matthew 2:11, and the church is called God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and a chosen people who declare the praises of Him who called them out of darkness into His light, 1 Peter 2:9. The nations stream to the light by faith and not to a physical city, which fits what Jesus says in John 4:21-24.

views.label: In a future restored Jerusalem and then the new creation
views.case: Some readers expect a literal future city in which the nations come to honour the LORD, as in Zechariah 8:20-23, followed by the new heavens and earth. They point to the details that the first return did not fulfil, such as the end of violence in verse 18 and a people all righteous in verse 21.

debates.bearing: These readings are often held together. The chapter had a partial fulfilment in the return, a deeper one in Christ and the gathering of the nations to Him, and its final form appears in Revelation 21 and 22, where John uses its images for the new Jerusalem. Whatever view one takes, the light is the LORD Himself and the nations come to Him, not to the city for its own sake.

debates.question: How should we read the nations serving Zion, and the destruction of those who will not, in verses 12 and 14?

views.label: A reversal of oppression, in the language of the ancient world
views.case: Israel had been oppressed by nations, and the prophet speaks in the royal and military vocabulary people knew, in which kings bow and tribute is paid. The point is that Israel's humiliation will be reversed. Isaiah 49:23 uses the same picture of kings bowing and licking the dust.

views.label: Submission to the LORD, whose glory rests on Zion
views.case: The service is not to Israel as a nation in itself but to the LORD whose glory is on the city. Verse 14 says they call her 'the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel', and verse 9 says the wealth is brought 'to the honor of the LORD your God.' The nations who refuse are refusing God.

views.label: A picture fulfilled in the gospel by grace, not conquest
views.case: In Christ the nations come willingly and are welcomed as fellow citizens, Ephesians 2:19. The strong language of verse 12 points to the seriousness of refusing the light, but the way into the city is open, as the open gates of verse 11 show.

debates.bearing: The chapter holds welcome and warning together. The gates never close, which means the invitation is wide, yet to remain outside the light is to remain in darkness, and that is the meaning of the sentence in verse 12.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with two imperatives to a feminine singular 'you', qumi, 'arise', and ori, 'shine', from the same root as 'light', or. The command to shine is built from the noun that follows, so that the people are asked to become what has arrived. Then the verb for what the glory does, 'rises', is zarach, the verb used of the sun rising, as at Exodus 22:3 and Psalm 104:22. Verse 2 repeats the verb for the LORD, 'will rise upon you', so that Zion is told that the LORD Himself is her sunrise. In other words, 'light' (or), 'glory' (kavod) and 'rise' (zarach) belong to one image, the dawning of God's presence. Verse 3 adds the brightness (nogah) of the dawn which draws kings.

The word 'glory' in verses 1 and 2 is kavod, from a root with the sense of weight. It appears in verse 7 as God's decision to 'adorn My glorious house', where the verb pa'ar means to beautify, and in verse 13 as the 'glory of Lebanon', the cypress, elm and boxwood timber. The one root is therefore applied to the LORD's presence, to His house and to the finest materials of the nations, and the passage means that the best things of the nations are drawn into the worship of the One whose glory is the greatest. Verse 13 speaks of 'the place of My feet', which echoes the place of His throne and the soles of His feet, where He promised to dwell among Israel forever, Ezekiel 43:7.

In verse 7 the sacrifices go up on God's altar 'with acceptance', and in verse 10 God says that 'in favor' He will show mercy. Both phrases use ratzon, favour or acceptance, the same noun that will appear in Isaiah 61:2 in 'the year of the LORD's favor'. Acceptance at the altar, mercy after anger and the year of favor are one idea, God's pleasure turned toward His people. The reader who goes from chapter 60 into 61 is meeting the same word again.

Verse 17 contains a small piece of irony. The BSB has 'I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler'. The word for 'ruler' is nogesh, which is also the word for the taskmasters of Egypt, as in Exodus 5:6, 'Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people.' So the harsh overseers of old are replaced by righteousness itself, and the very term that meant oppression now means the authority that guards the city. The vocabulary of slavery is used to describe the new rule.

Verse 21 calls the people 'the branch of My planting, the work of My hands'. The picture is of a shoot that God Himself has planted, which recalls the Branch from Jesse's roots in Isaiah 11:1, and Isaiah 61:3 will take up the planting language again in 'the planting of the LORD'. The people are a shoot God Himself has planted for His glory. In verse 16 the LORD describes Himself as Savior and Redeemer, the goel, the same title for the one who comes to Zion in Isaiah 59:20, so that chapter 60 shows what that Redeemer's coming brings.

The last verse holds a tension in the Hebrew itself. 'In its time' (be'ittah) points to the right season set by God, and 'quickly' (from chush, to hasten) points to speed when that moment arrives. God does not hurry according to human calendars, but when the time comes He acts without delay.

typology.type: The nations bringing gold and frankincense, verses 5 to 6
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah describes camel caravans bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD. In Matthew 2:11 Magi from the east come to the house, fall down, worship and offer gold, frankincense and myrrh. Matthew does not quote Isaiah 60, so the link is an echo and not a stated fulfilment, but the gifts, the east and the worship all line up, and Herod's disturbance shows the contrast, Matthew 2:3. The escalation is that the nations come not to a city but to a child, who is Himself the glory of the LORD. The type falls short in that Isaiah foresees whole peoples arriving, while Matthew shows only the first few, and the full gathering waits for Revelation 21:24-26.

typology.type: The glory that rises, verses 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: The LORD's glory rises on Zion like a sunrise. Luke 1:78-79 speaks of the Dawn visiting from on high to shine on those in darkness, and John writes that the true Light was coming into the world, John 1:9. Jesus says 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. The Old Testament gave a glory that came to the tabernacle and temple and then left, Ezekiel 10:18-19. Christ is the glory of God in a person, who does not depart and who is not confined to a building. The pattern falls short because the earlier glory was seen by one nation in one place, whereas the light of Christ is meant for the ends of the earth, Acts 13:47.

typology.type: The open gates and the glorious house, verses 7, 11 and 13
typology.fulfillment: The temple is adorned, the gates never shut, and the wealth of nations comes in. Isaiah 56:7 had said the house would be called a house of prayer for all nations. Jesus quotes that line in cleansing the temple, Mark 11:17, and so claims it as His own purpose. Paul says that Gentiles are no longer strangers but are being built into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:19-22. In Revelation 21:22 there is no temple in the city because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The first temple was a building that needed gates and guards. The final one is God's presence itself, and the gates stand open because there is no night to fear, Revelation 21:25.

typology.type: Everlasting light replacing sun and moon, verses 19 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The LORD Himself is the city's light. John makes the correspondence nearly exact: the city has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23, and there is no more night, Revelation 22:5. The escalation is that Isaiah says 'the LORD' and John says 'God and the Lamb', placing Christ at the centre of the light. In the interval, believers are children of light, Ephesians 5:8, who carry a share of that light into the present darkness, Matthew 5:14. The type falls short because the sun and moon are still necessary now, and the promise belongs to the age when former things have passed away, Revelation 21:4.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most directly through its central image. The glory of the LORD rises on a darkened world, and the New Testament says that this happened in a person. Zechariah's song speaks of 'the Dawn' visiting from on high to shine on those who live in darkness, Luke 1:78-79. Simeon holds the infant and calls Him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel', Luke 2:32, joining the two halves of Isaiah 60, the nations drawn and Zion glorified. John says that the true Light was coming into the world, John 1:9. Jesus Himself says 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and 'I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness,' John 12:46.

The Magi in Matthew 2 show the link on the ground. Gentiles from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the King of the Jews has been born, and then bring gold and frankincense to the child. Herod and 'all Jerusalem with him' are disturbed, Matthew 2:3. The contrast is deliberate. The city that was told to arise and shine is troubled by the arrival of the light, while foreigners kneel before it. Matthew is not saying that the Magi fulfil all of Isaiah 60, only that the pattern of the nations coming to the light has begun, and that the One they come to is greater than the city.

Christ is also the one who makes Zion's promised righteousness possible. Verse 21 says the people will all be righteous, which the first return could not deliver. Paul says that Christ became to us righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30, and that God has made us a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The gates open because of Him: Jesus calls Himself the door, John 10:9, and the way, John 14:6. The temple of verses 7 and 13 is found in Him, John 2:19-21, and then in His people.

The end of the chapter is fulfilled in the vision of the new Jerusalem. John writes that the city has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God illuminates it and the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The Lamb is at the heart of the light. Isaiah promised that the LORD Himself would be everlasting light, and John shows that this is Christ, who is God with us.

A caution keeps the reading faithful. Isaiah 60 is addressed to Zion and describes a restored city and a redeemed people; the New Testament does not treat every detail as a prophecy about the infant Jesus. The camels of Midian and the ships of Tarshish are not hidden codes. What the writers take up is the movement of the passage, God's glory arriving, the nations drawn, and the LORD as the light. And even the severe verse 12 is to be read alongside the open gates of verse 11 and the words of Jesus that whoever follows Him will never walk in darkness, John 8:12.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He is the source of light and not merely its reflector. Zion is told to shine only because the light has already come, and the light is His own glory, which rises over her. There is nothing in Zion that produces it. The final verses make the point complete: she will no longer need sun or moon, because 'the LORD will be your everlasting light.' God is the self-sufficient radiance in whom everything else is seen.

God is also the God who gathers. The sons and daughters are carried home, the nations bring their wealth, and the ships of Tarshish lead the way. Verse 22 says that He will do this Himself: 'I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly.' The great reversal is not left to chance or to political fortune. The God who scattered Israel is the God who brings her back, and He does so in His own time.

The chapter holds anger and favour together. 'I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy,' verse 10. The wording does not hide the earlier judgment and does not allow it to be the last word. Verse 15 describes the reversal in terms of a person who was forsaken and passed by, and now becomes an everlasting pride. Judgment and mercy come from the same holy love, and the history of the exile shows that God is serious about sin and slow to leave His people in it.

He is a God of generous restoration. The metals are replaced by better ones, verse 17, and the oppressors are replaced by peace and righteousness, so that He does not merely return what was lost but improves it. He also acts for His own glory: He will glorify the place of His feet, adorn His house, and make the people the work of His hands, 'so that I may be glorified.' This is not self-centredness in a bad sense. The glory of God is the highest good, and to be brought into it is to be brought into the greatest joy.

He is the God of all nations. Midian, Sheba, Kedar and Tarshish are not mere onlookers, and God receives their offerings. He is also the Holy One of Israel, Savior, Redeemer and Mighty One of Jacob, verse 16, and these titles keep the particular and the universal together. For worship, the chapter calls His people to look up and to look out. Look up to the light that has risen, and look around to see who is coming, so that praise rises with the nations as the caravans proclaim 'the praises of the LORD,' verse 6.

crossReferences.note: The invitation to lift up your eyes and see the gathering children and the kings who bow is first given here. Isaiah 60:4 repeats the words, so that chapter 60 reads as the fuller arrival of what chapter 49 promised. The reader sees that Isaiah's promises are woven together across the book.

The people walking in darkness have seen a great light. Isaiah 60:1-2 enlarges the same picture so that the light is the LORD's glory rising over a darkened world. Matthew quotes Isaiah 9:2 of Jesus in Galilee, Matthew 4:15-16, joining the two chapters to Christ.

In the last days all nations stream to the mountain of the LORD to be taught His ways. Isaiah 60 gives the scene colour and detail, with caravans, ships and timber, and brings out the point that the nations come as worshippers. The beginning and the later part of the book share this one hope.

Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will have their offerings accepted on His altar, and His house will be called a house of prayer for all nations. Isaiah 60:7 shows the flocks of Kedar and Nebaioth going up on that altar with acceptance, which is the same promise seen in action.

God promises to shake the nations so that their treasures come in and fill the house with glory, greater than the former. Written to a discouraged community looking at a modest temple, it parallels Isaiah 60:5-7 and 13, and shows that the same hope was held out to the returned exiles.

The queen of Sheba arrives with camels bearing spices and gold, an earlier and smaller picture of what Isaiah 60:6 describes. Solomon's court was a partial sign of the nations drawn by the wisdom of the God of Israel, and the prophet expects a greater coming.

Magi from the east come asking for the born King, and offer gold and frankincense, while Jerusalem is disturbed. The pattern of Isaiah 60, the nations come with treasure to the light, is seen in the first weeks of Jesus' life, though Matthew does not cite the chapter himself.

Simeon calls the child 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.' The two halves of Isaiah 60, the nations drawn by the light and Zion made glorious, are joined in one sentence. It shows how the first believers read the chapter as being fulfilled in Jesus.

Jesus says 'I am the light of the world' and promises that whoever follows Him will not walk in darkness. In claiming this He steps into the place the LORD takes in Isaiah 60:19, as the everlasting light, and offers to people now what the chapter promises to a city.

Gentiles are no longer strangers but fellow citizens, built into a holy temple where God dwells by His Spirit. This is the present form of Isaiah 60:10 and 13, where foreigners build and bring timber for the house, and the church is the community in which the promise is taking shape.

No temple, no sun or moon, the Lamb as lamp, the nations walking by the light, the kings bringing their glory, the gates never shut. John reads Isaiah 60:3, 11, 19 and 20 together in the new Jerusalem and shows the final form of the promise.

There is no more night and no need of lamp or sun, because the Lord God will shine on His people. It repeats Isaiah 60:19-20 in a final sentence and links the light with reigning forever, so that the end of darkness is also the end of exile.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with light, 'Let there be light,' Genesis 1:3, and before the sun is made the light is already shining. From that start the story is a long struggle between light and dark. The fall brings darkness into human life, and the nations wander in it. Isaiah 60 speaks into that long night. It says that the darkness over the peoples will be met by the rising of the LORD Himself, and that what draws the nations is not Israel's strength but God's glory resting on her.

The chapter also answers a question left open by Abraham's call. God told him that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, but through most of the Old Testament the nations seem to stand outside, and Israel is small. Isaiah 60 shows how it will happen. The families of Abraham's other sons and of Ishmael arrive as worshippers, bringing their offerings, and the blessing spreads outward through the light. The people of Israel are meant to be a lamp, and the promise made in Genesis moves toward its fulfilment.

It stands, too, at the point where the story of exile turns to restoration. The city that was forsaken, with no one passing through, verse 15, is told it will be an everlasting pride. This does not mean that Israel's restoration was simple. The returned community was small and troubled, and later prophets said the greater glory was still to come, Haggai 2:9. The chapter therefore pulls the reader forward to Christ, the light of the world, in whom the nations begin to come, and to the church, which Paul describes as a temple built from Jew and Gentile together, Ephesians 2:19-22.

The new creation completes the picture. In Revelation 21 and 22 the city comes down from God with the glory of God, its radiance like a jewel. The gates are never shut, the nations walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it. The curse of Genesis 3 is gone, there is no more night, and the tree of life grows by the river, Revelation 22:2-5. What began as a command to one small city, 'Arise, shine,' ends as a world lit by the presence of God and the Lamb, and in that light the people He has gathered from every nation will see His face and reign with Him.

quiz.q: What is the reason Zion is told to arise and shine in verse 1?

options.text: Because her light has come and the glory of the LORD has risen upon her.
options.note: Verse 1 gives this as the direct cause for her shining.

options.text: Because she has achieved this glory through her own effort.
options.note: The light and glory are given by God, not self-generated.

options.text: Because the surrounding nations have finally been defeated militarily.
options.note: The chapter emphasizes God's glory rising upon her, not military conquest, as the cause.

options.text: Because darkness has been permanently removed from the whole earth already.
options.note: Verse 2 actually says darkness still covers the earth and peoples; it is Zion specifically who is lit by the LORD's rising glory, not the whole earth yet.

quiz.q: What connects this chapter to the Magi's visit in Matthew 2?

options.text: The gold and frankincense nations bring to Zion's light echo the Magi's gifts to the infant Jesus.
options.note: Verse 6's gold and frankincense closely match the Magi's gifts in Matthew 2:11.

options.text: There is no connection between the two passages.
options.note: The parallel in specific gifts, gold and frankincense, is a deliberate echo.

options.text: The Magi are explicitly named in Isaiah 60.
options.note: Isaiah speaks generally of nations and camels from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba, not the Magi by name.

options.text: The connection is only about camels, not gifts.
options.note: Camels do appear in both accounts' broader imagery, but the stronger, more specific connection is the shared gifts of gold and frankincense.

quiz.q: How does Revelation 21 use the language of Isaiah 60:19-20?

options.text: It describes the new Jerusalem needing no sun or moon because God's glory and the Lamb are its light, closely echoing this chapter.
options.note: Revelation 21:23-25 draws directly on this promise.

options.text: It rejects the idea of any everlasting light entirely.
options.note: Revelation affirms and fulfills this very promise.

options.text: It applies the promise only to the sun's literal astronomical behavior.
options.note: The sun and moon are named literally, but the language is about God's presence replacing the need for any created light source, a theological rather than purely astronomical claim.

options.text: It has no relationship to Isaiah's Old Testament promises.
options.note: Revelation 21 draws extensively and deliberately on Isaiah's imagery.

quiz.q: What does verse 17, 'I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler,' emphasize?

options.text: That Zion's future leadership and social order will be marked by peace and righteousness rather than violence.
options.note: This verse envisions transformed governance under God's reign.

options.text: That Zion will have no leaders or governance structure at all.
options.note: The verse describes peace and righteousness personified as governing, not the absence of order.

options.text: That literal precious metals will replace all forms of government.
options.note: The verse does mention precious metals just before this clause, but that is a separate image of material blessing; peace and righteousness as ruler describe governance, not currency.

options.text: That foreign kings will rule over Zion permanently.
options.note: The passage describes God appointing peace and righteousness, not foreign domination, as Zion's governance.

questions: Zion is told to arise and shine because her light has come, not because she generated it herself. Where in your life are you trying to manufacture light or glory that only God can give?
Nations streamed toward Zion's light bringing their best treasures. What is the best thing you have to offer in worship to God, and are you actually bringing it?
God says though He struck Zion in anger, He would show her mercy and glorify her beyond her former shame. Where do you need to trust that God's discipline in your life is not His last word?
The chapter promises peace and righteousness as governor and ruler. What would change in your relationships or community if you let peace and righteousness genuinely govern your decisions this week?
This chapter's fullest promise is fulfilled in Revelation, where God Himself is everlasting light and sorrow ends. How does that future certainty change how you carry present darkness or sorrow?

translationNotes.note: Midian, Ephah, and Sheba name Arabian trading regions known for spices and precious goods; the picture is of the ancient world's wealthiest caravan routes converging on Zion.
